items.title: Deadlines
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
Sometimes you stop writing for a while, start writing a piece about why you haven't been writing, and then fail to finish it for so long that your surroundings get back to a state where you actually feel like writing again.

That's basically what happened with this post, which I started drafting shortly after the trade deadline in August (hence the title). A lot of deadlines—personal and otherwise—have passed since then, and this has evolved with them to become significantly less morose than its first few iterations. Most of the original material isn't worth presenting anymore, but I'll retain the brief recap of the biggest events that kept me largely out of commission over the summer:

  • After finishing grad school, I had to go to physical therapy for a super-duper fun (read: agonizing) shoulder issue that I alluded to in the vaguest of terms . Thankfully, PT helped a lot, but it put a huge damper on any sort of writing efforts (and pretty much everything else).
  • I moved out of Boston and back to North Carolina, which tragically necessitated spending a day or two sorting all of my baseball cards so I could get rid of a bunch of them to try and fit everything in my not-very-large car.
  • I presented my expanded master’s thesis at ! It was a blast, except for the part where I was frantically finishing my slides a couple hours before my presentation while simultaneously trying to listen to a panel discussion. 

You may notice a few changes to the site, most notably the absence of the donation page that previously graced the navigation header. That's because I have an honest-to-goodness full-time job! It's no longer breaking news, but I'm still very excited to tell you all that I am now a software engineer with , a company that needs no introduction to anyone who reads this blog. I have less time to write than I used to, especially since I'm still writing for BP, but I also don't have to spend a ton of time and energy worrying about employment, which is better for the creative spirit. (It helps that it's a really great job on all fronts.)

Okay, enough personal updates! I'm not planning to go through the recent rash of signings in too much depth, but while we're all here, I may as well address the herd of elephants in the room.

Around 4:45 PM last Sunday, despite wanting to do basically anything else, I left my house and drove down to Target in the pouring rain for a long-overdue errand. At 5:01, I parked, killed the engine, and opened my phone to a dozen group chat messages and an headline that read Mets To Sign Tarik Skubal. I kept my wits about me long enough to break the news to my father, which went as follows (verbatim):

Then I got out of the car, hustled across the quarter mile of pavement between me and dry land, and wandered around the store for far longer than necessary in a haze of disbelief. I'm sure you probably experienced something similar upon hearing the terms of the deal. As one of the wonderful editors at , , put it,

Over the course of the next nine years, will receive gross pay equal to almost half the gate receipts for Shrek 2

And who's mad about it? Sure as hell not me!

Yeah, I could get a head start on catastrophizing, but... as much as I've said over the past several months that I don't want him—that I barely want us to sign because they'll just be tainted by the curse—it feels a little different now that it's actually real. Maybe we will ruin him somehow. Maybe we won't. It's hard to be pessimistic about everything forever, even if it the Mets. Plus I'm trying to practice better mental habits, like not worrying about future events that are totally outside my sphere of influence, and last I checked I don't work for the Mets pitching lab.

has done a fantastic job assembling the full context of the deal in , which I highly recommend to anyone who wants far more regular and in-depth updates on the Mets than I can provide. Some of the more interesting tidbits beyond the contract itself:

  • The traditional introductory press conference is penciled in for December 1, right before The Lockout is supposed to start, so mark your calendars.
  • The Blue Jays were indeed all in on Skubal, offering $420 million over the same nine years. It's a good thing the Mets were willing to keep upping their price, because it would take a lot of money for most reasonable people to relocate to Canada.
  • The Dodgers, on the other hand, were all but out, allegedly gesturing to the CBA negotiations as a vague excuse to not spend money. That's also how I would defend myself if I were a coward and hated fun.

Will Sammon at provided some into the negotiations that highlighted why our famously pitcher-shy front office was more eager to take the plunge than usual:

Skubal lucidly outlined items of importance, from family concerns to aspects of winning. He impressed Mets officials with his discipline when the pitcher detailed his workouts. When he spoke about the Mets, he didn’t just tick off the obvious components of the roster; Skubal rattled off names of pitchers in the farm system. He had done his homework. He showed up prepared, interested. He struck Mets officials as sincere, articulate.

I'm not sure he had to study much to assure them of his sincerity. seems like sufficient proof that he's long since embraced the local culture:

I mean, can you blame him?

I already know I'm going to spend all year getting confused when people talk about , because "Goldy" is already a guy to me. His name is Aaron Goldsmith. He does fantastic play-by-play work for the Mariners. And I'm sorry, but if there is any justice in the universe, he'll take up a lot more broadcast time on my screen than Paul does.

Goldy 2.0 is joining the Mets on a one-year, $8 million contract to (presumably) do what he does best: platoon. You'll hear about his ability to hit lefties over the coming months, and for good reason; I won't be the first person to mention most of his stats, so I'll skip the paraphrasing and just quote directly. From Roger Cormier:

Goldschmidt, the 2022 NL MVP, was indeed a left-handed pitcher’s nightmare in 2026 while playing for New York (AL). He hit for a .967 OPS in 183 plate appearances against them. And it isn’t a fluke: his career OPS against southpaws is 1.004.

Forty-seven players have faced southpaws 500 times or more in the last three years, and among them, only two⁠—Jose Ramírez and Ketel Marte⁠—have a higher OPS than Goldschmidt’s .930.

For my part, I'll point out that despite Goldschmidt's recent struggles against righties, he has never finished a season with a wRC+ under 100. Even at the age of 38 last year, his numbers against lefties were exceptional in all sorts of ways: .299/.393/.573, 12% walk rate vs. 18% strikeout rate, .411 wOBA, and 168 wRC+.

Cormier also notes that Goldschmidt has been unusually healthy throughout his career—knock on wood—and reportedly a positive presence in the clubhouse. There's still quite a bit of risk involved, of course, but a Goldschmidt/ platoon (best wishes for his recovery!) at least has the potential to be pretty solid. It also makes look even more like trade bait after being tendered a contract.

Rather than putting it off like they did with Skubal, the Mets for Goldschmidt via Zoom on Wednesday. If you don't feel like watching, he recited the usual lines about joining a great organization that really wants to win and wanting to help the team however he can even if he isn't playing every day, yadda yadda yadda. In line with what other veterans like Soto have expressed, Goldschmidt said he was excited about the bumper crop of young talent and the possibility of being a mentor in the clubhouse. He also mentioned his existing connection with manager Andy Green, who crossed paths with him as the Diamondbacks' third-base coach in 2015 (Green also managed several of their minor-league affiliates from 2012–14, when Goldschmidt was in the majors).

Oh, and he's just as thrilled about Skubal as everyone else.

The remaining Mets transactions of note:

A number of old friends have moved to new places:

And last but not least, a couple updates from the Mariners:

  • The headliner here is the involving , who's joining Seattle alongside and in exchange for sending , , and to the Royals. This is an interesting (if mildly confusing) move that I like for the most part; Patrick Dubuque wrote up a nice analysis of it at BP. The major upsides, in my eyes:
    • Garcia is an exceptional fielder. Prior to 2025, he wasn't really much good on the other side of the ball, and the potential effects of T-Mobile Park on his bat are a meaningful concern, but I'm just going to be optimistic about that for now.
    • I no longer have to see Bryce Miller pitch for the Mariners. (Unfortunately, I might have to see him pitch for the Royals, who I sometimes tune into to see and .)
  • The organization is also reuniting with on a with an invite to spring training. My friends who are long-term Mariners fans have informed me that he was one of the creators of their little infield dance celebration and are very excited about this development.

Have a good weekend! I'll see you when I see you.

items.title: I made a daily word game!
items.author: bounces+lmurrlxe4wcmh40rlxqc6h8843rv9igh75wl@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This is a short week and a holiday, so I'm doing something a little different for this week's newsletter: I'm telling you about Foreword, the free daily word game I made!

It's inspired by Scattergories and Wordle and is a really quick, fun way to spend a couple minutes every day. You can play solo or in groups with friends and family.

Each day, you get the day's letter (today's is "R") and 10 prompts like "Rainy day activities" or "Children's games" or "Magazines". You have two minutes to answer as many prompts as possible using words that start with the day's letter. You can even get multiple points for a single prompt if your answer has multiple words that start with the day's letter (like "Peppa Pig" for "Cartoon characters").

Each game is graded by Fred, a pretty opinionated AI judge who can be a little snarky and appreciates creativity.

I built Foreword because ... well because I wanted it to exist. I enjoy word games like Catch Phrase, Taboo, and Scattergories, and I play daily word games like Wordle, crosswords, and some NYT daily games. I thought, "Wouldn't it be fun to a daily word game that I can play with friends?" And I was off to the races.

I've been playing every day for a few months, and there are about 70 people who play it each day now. Most people are in a group or two with friends and family, where they can see each other's answers and even react to them when they're funny (😂) or brilliant (💡) or suspect (🧐). Playing in groups is my favorite thing about Foreword, so start a group and invite some folks to join you!

People have really been enjoying it, so I hope you'll check it out!

Here's my result from today:

Have a Happy Thanksgiving and enjoy the long weekend!

PS Tomorrow is Thanksgiving and I've got some fun surprises in store. So make sure you play Foreword tomorrow!

items.title: A Royals Offseason Roadmap, Dictated by the Market
items.author: SRS0=Dv60=JO=mg-d0.substack.com=bounce+9ddca1.63af5d-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
A fitting baseball offseason colloquialism leading into Thanksgiving.

As November dawns and World Series winners wrestle hangovers, the rest of the baseball world turns to the hot stove and, well, shopping lists. Digital ink is spilled on each club’s needs and how to best fulfill them, as if Major League Baseball, its clubs and free agents exist in a static roster-building simulation.

Sign a starting pitcher. Check the box. Move on to the next priority. (Need two? The Boras Corp. Corner Store is offering a buy-one-get-one blowout sale!)

But how roster construction really works — best I can tell, as someone prognosticating from a spare basement bedroom rather than pulling strings from a plush front office swivel chair — is less like a trip to the grocery store and more like a quest to buy the perfect used car.

What starts as a need (lane assist, or a free agent left-handed starting pitcher) can quickly become a want — or out of reach entirely. Budgets are set beforehand but might be stretched for just the right fit. Maybe your scouts love a certain make/model but your manager (spouse? this metaphor is getting worse) prefers a sturdier build.

Most importantly, the market drives everything. The car you dreamed of costs more than you expected, or it isn’t available in your area, or interest rates leap, or the rest of the league decides paying a premium for starting pitching is what’s required with a lockout looming.

In all likelihood, the Royals envisioned themselves — maybe as recently as two weeks ago — largely filling out their rotation through free agency. It’s not a stretch to make that assumption. Seth Lugo and Michael Wacha are the prime examples.

As negotiations opened earlier this month, my hunch is it became clear the organization would not be partaking in the sweepstakes for starters in the second tier of the market behind Tarik Skubal. Two candidates, left-hander Trevor Rogers and right-hander Freddy Peralta, each signed for five years this week; Rogers for $120 million, Peralta for $125 million.

Many projections pegged each of the two for four-year agreements in the $75-100 million range, a far cry from the deals they’d eventually sign.

And if my guess is correct, Kansas City realized its intention to splash cash at starting pitching would not provide the optimal route to contention.

The market shifted. So did the Royals.

Instead, they dealt third baseman Maikel Garcia — just one year into a long-term contract — as part of a package that included reliever James McArthur and minor league lefty LP Langevin for a haul of MLB-ready arms: RHP Bryce Miller, a high-upside starter; LHP Jose A. Ferrer, a ground-ball inducing bullpen weapon; and RHP Logan Evans, who profiles as a back-end starting pitcher and innings eater.

I love Garcia

Shove+ grades

Shove+ is my pitching model (limited to starting pitchers only, for now) that seeks to identify talent over production, using metrics like Stuff+, CSW% and Location+ to balance skill, control and ability to limit damage on contact.

Based on 2026 evaluations, Miller will head into 2027 as the club’s most talented starter — by far.

A lot of conclusions are being drawn that the club is operating from a desire to avoid spending money, instead choosing to deal from its cache of young, talented hitters to fill a rotation. Robbing Peter to pay Paul, in a sense.

Those conclusions are being drawn in haste. It is Nov. 25. The offseason is just beginning, particularly in regard to free-agent hitters, few of which have signed while arms (Skubal, Rogers, Peralta, old friend Kris Bubic, Dustin May, Sonny Gray, Kaima Taira) dominate headlines.

Perhaps my entire thesis is incorrect, and Kansas City always intended to trade for pitching then turn to free agency to fill holes in the lineup.

But my hunch is the club sought to ink free agents to shore up most of its weaknesses (starting pitching, bullpen, left field, center field) and quickly learned the price of the buck had gone up on starting pitching. Damn tariffs.

Either way, the next move to watch for is possibly a multi-year agreement with one of the impact hitters, such as left fielders Seiya Suzuki, Randy Arozarena, Ian Happ or Taylor Ward. Signing any of these four will, in all likelihood, cost much less both long-term and in 2027 than the crop of starting pitchers already off the board.

The market dictated the direction of this early stage of the offseason, as it so often does. The Royals adjusted. Let’s give them some time before determining whether that pivot in approach will be rewarded.

items.title: A Wild Week at One Royal Way
items.author: SRS0=OXl3=JM=mg-d1.substack.com=bounce+5f4299.39b08c6-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
I didn’t have the Royals pegged as the team that would make the first big splash in the trade market this off-season, but that’s exactly what happened last Wednesday.

Early that morning reports started circulating that JJ Picollo was dangling former All-Star 3B Maikel Garcia in trade talks to bolster their pitching staff for 2027.

Public opinion about the deal among both KC and Seattle fans on social media was all over the place …

I love the deal, with one caveat we’ll discuss in a minute

After the deal was announced, some of the local radio talking heads said that even the Royals had grown weary of Garcia’s questionable work ethic and effort level on the field.

I’m not sure Garcia’s on-field performance in Kansas City was all that either. Yes, he had a terrific 2025 season. The Royals should have traded him a year ago when his value was as high as it likely will ever be. Instead, JJ Picollo gave Garcia a $52M contract extension and we all watched him struggle through a very bad and injury-plagued 2026 season.

Garcia obviously provided excellent defense at third base, and that will not be easy to replace. The point is that Garcia’s body of work with the bat is not what a lot of Royals fans seem to think. It will be fascinating to see how he does in Seattle’s notoriously poor hitting ballpark.

Let’s look at the other two players the Royals gave up, as well as the three they received from Seattle…

In addition to Garcia Seattle gets…

Of course you can’t assume a guy who hasn’t pitched above High A is going to exert the same kind of dominance in the majors, but fastballs like Langevin’s don’t grow on trees folks. It’s a sign of JJ Picollo’s urgency to win in 2027 that a reliever-starved organization traded their best relief prospect for some immediate help.

Seattle thought highly enough of Ferrer to trade their 2021 first round draft pick (Harry Ford) for him a year ago. My favorite description of Ferrer so far…”He’s like Angel Zerpa if Zerpa was good at pitching”.

Kudos to JJ for recognizing that it made sense to move Garcia, but I sure wish he could have gotten it done without involving Langevin.

Not gonna lie, this one hurts. Izzy has long been a DC favorite, dating all the way back to the 2021 Pre-Season Manifesto where I predicted he would be the AL Rookie of the Year. Isbel broke camp with the big club that spring, but hit his way back to Omaha and only played in 28 big league games.

Since that time Isbel has been the quasi-regular center fielder. His defense has always been elite, but the bat just never blossomed like we all hoped. He finishes his KC career with a .235/.284/.357 slash line. Ultimately I think the on base percentage did him in.

I don’t think that Roccaforte is going to just be given the every day job in CF, but the free agent market is pretty slim. I’ve seen some speculation that the Royals could bring back Lane Thomas to platoon with Rocco. I don’t hate that idea.

The Royals still have a glaring need for a RH impact bat in the outfield, and they only have 8 days to get something done before a labor lockout is imposed on Dec. 2nd.

Could be another wild week in store at One Royal Way.

Let me know in the comments what you think about the Garcia trade!

items.title: Award: Here for It, #368
items.author: SRS0=2yBh=JM=m.ghost.io=bounce+3cffae.7bdc18-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Hi! It's R. Eric Thomas. From the internet?Hi!

I feel sure that I've written about my deep love of awards shows in this newsletter before but I cannot find it and so maybe I dreamt it. Maybe I've dreamt this entire newsletter!

(It's truly amazing how much useless stuff I get done in my dreams. Last week, I attended an entire conference in my dream. My schedule included plenaries and an award dinner. A man next to me at the award dinner repeatedly told me that he was playing "John Travolta in He seemed very proud of it. I was not and am not sure if he was playing John Travolta in a movie about the making of or if he was just playing the John Travolta role in the 1999 stage adaptation of said film. What's crazy about dreams is that there is no way for me to find the answers to this question because it all came from inside my head, objectively a confusing and chaotic environment!)

Anyway, my favorite award show is the Barrymores, the regional theater awards for the Philadelphia community. I've gone to the Barrymores since 2013 and it's consistently one of the highlights of my year. (And I include the year I won a Barrymore and also the year I ate something I was allergic to at the afterparty, went into anaphylactic shock and had to go to the emergency room. It's called having range!)

In 2013, I was a marketing assistant at a local theater company and I somehow got to go to the Theatre Prom, and I had a transformational experience.

I'd spent the previous 7 years in Philadelphia trying to make in-roads into the community and often feeling like I was failing at it. What I realized that night was that being a part of the community wasn't about one particular place or accomplishment or career milestone. It was on-going and ever-changing and, at that moment, was centered around wearing my one (1) suit and devouring the mac and cheese buffet.

Three years later, I'd win a Barrymore Award for Best New Play. That was a great night, but--no shade--there was no mac and cheese bar and so the overall experience was a mixed bag.

I've since been nominated six more times but never won again. (Yes, the authorities are looking into it. We're expecting charges from the Justice Department any day.) But I go back every year because I think of the "Theatre Prom" more as a wedding.

You go to a wedding to celebrate the couple, sure, but at the best weddings you're also reminded of the beauty of your own life and your own love and your own joy and the privilege of being with people you love and strangers who love the same thing you love. And you get a free meal and an open bar if you want it and you're wearing fancy clothes and you get to hear the Cha-Cha Slide which, shockingly, one does not encounter in everyday life. And that's what you're really there for.

I love enthusiasm. And I love the improbable idea that that which you love can somehow love you back.

And so it was improbable and lovely in equal measure that my friend Robi Hager texted me and told me that he was directing this year's Barrymore Awards and that he had a big, ambitious vision and part of that vision was me hosting.

He said, "I want you to be Neil Patrick Harris at the Tonys."

The Barrymores were last week and, beloved, let me tell you--this was the hardest thing I've ever done professionally and I once had an emotionally ruinous Zoom call with Lee Daniels, director of

It was also one of the highlights of my life (the Barrymores. Not that Zoom. Sheesh!)

Robi wanted me to co-write an opening number in addition to doing a comic monologue to start the show. I said, "I don't sing and dance." He said, "I believe in you," and, alas, people believing in me is my Kryptonite.

I co-wrote an opening song with Jake Collins and then rehearsed a performance choreographed by Devon Sinclair. Y'all, they had ya boy out here doing time steps! (And if you don't know what a time step is, you and I are the same! I have neither a formal theater education nor significant lung capacity. Ya boy was on life support!)

Erik Larson immediately saw the vision and decided to design and hand-make six different outfits for me to wear. Every time I hit the stage, I was in a different look.

Erik quipped that I was Neil Patrick Hairless. And our friend Alex followed up with Neil Black-trick Harris. And I've spent the entire weekend trying to come up with a third play on words. The best I can do is Key and Peele Patrick Harris but I want you to know that I'm not proud of it and I'm not happy about it.

Every single moment was simultaneously so hard and so revelatory. Robi and Erik and Devon and Jake saw something in me that I didn't. I have no problem hosting something. It doesn't feel haughty to say I'm good at holding a mic and telling jokes and occasionally running a live auction. If I'm doing a book event, we're going to have a great time. But singing, dancing, starting a kick-line on the correct foot, doing a quick change, doing six quick changes--all of that felt ambitious.

I'm an ambitious person but I'm also lazy. But I like being around people who have large ambitions, because it makes your ambitions seem right-sized. It makes you want to expand, to do and dream and achieve more. And that feels like magic.

If I'm challenged by people who have my back and can guide me when I don't know where to go, the challenge can elevate me as opposed to stymieing me.

There's nothing wrong with a challenge, but you need support, mentorship, and other people who get the idea. I love to be around people whose ambitions outpace mine because then I think, "why am I dreaming so small? It's my life. How dare I put a limit on any part of it?"

It's important to make a fuss; it's important to put a marker in time and say "I was here and it was hard or it was easy or it was fun or there was free mac and cheese." It's important to care. And sometimes that means just showing up and enjoying yourself and sometimes that means putting a gigantic bow on your butt and joining a kick-line. Congratulations to everyone who is trying, including the random guy from my dream. Can't wait to see , whatever that means.

Tickets for Variety Pack: Volume 4 are now on sale! Four days, twelve shows, all comedy! Come check us out January 14-18, 2027!

items.content: Prather: One of the things that our survey reveals is what happens in between these elections. What you can see is a decline over time. So, much of the loss in trust among Republicans happened in the intervening years, not as a result of the election itself. So if you just looked at where Republican trust was post-2024 and then looked at it post-2026, you'd see this huge, massive decline. Most of that decline happened across January and then January to September, and really we only see a 6-percentage-point decline in trust from September to November. So that suggests to us there's something going on that's different.
